question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. The Act restricts fees for paying rent by electronic methods, and it applies to "a person", not only the landlord or agent. The retrieved excerpts don't settle every detail, though, so the points below are a guide, not a definitive ruling.

**What the law says**

- Your landlord or their agent must make sure a payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. The only costs allowed are bank or account fees on your own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Your landlord or agent must give you information about any costs you may incur from a payment method, including third-party transaction fees, before you agree to use that method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A person must not charge a renter a fee "in relation to the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- A person, other than an ADI (authorised deposit-taking institution, such as a bank), must not demand or receive a fee for any "prescribed matter" in relation to paying rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The Regulations' standard form says the rental provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees) and must allow Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

Probably not, based on the wording. The fee-prohibition provisions say "a person", so the fee going to the payments company rather than the agent doesn't obviously take it outside the Act. The main obligations on fee-free methods are placed on the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether the payments company, which isn't the landlord or agent, can be directly liable isn't addressed in the retrieved material. Whether the card fee is a "prescribed matter" under s 51A is also not shown in these excerpts, because the regulations listing prescribed matters for that section aren't included.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask your agent in writing for the card fee's amount and who receives it, and confirm which payment methods they consider fee-free. They must give you cost information before you agree to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask them to confirm that the bank transfer option is available to you. The law requires a no-extra-cost method to be "reasonably available," but the excerpts don't say how quickly it must be processed, so the slower speed doesn't by itself make it unavailable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If you're charged a fee you believe is unlawful, you can raise it with Consumer Affairs Victoria. The Act sets penalties for these breaches, but the excerpts don't describe the complaint or enforcement process.

**Sources and versions**

- The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file labelled version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, file labelled version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved text is labelled with these version numbers in the document metadata. The text itself does not state an "Authorised Version" number, so I can't confirm the number beyond that metadata.

The fee-prohibition provisions say "a person", so the fee going to the payments company rather than the agent doesn't obviously take it outside the Act.' question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether you must pay for a professional cleaner. They do say the landlord can only require professional cleaning in limited cases, and the test depends on the condition report and fair wear and tear. Your evidence of the carpets' condition is probably the key issue.

I've applied the current versions: the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), Authorised Version **009**, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **115**, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't include the wording of the standard form that applied when your lease started in 2024, so I can't confirm whether that version differed.

**What the law says**

- The landlord must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started and you were told so, or professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition, having regard to the condition report and taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The standard-form term says you must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Under the Act, a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A pet clause that goes beyond the standard-form term may be invalid [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You must leave the premises "in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession… taking into account fair wear and tear" and, as far as practicable, reasonably clean [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord can claim bond for cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, "having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check your start-of-tenancy condition report.** Compare the carpets' noted condition, and whether they were noted as clean, with what you found at the end. The Act says a condition report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition on the day it specifies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord must complete the end-of-tenancy report within 10 days after the agreement ends and give you a chance to attend if possible [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the agent in writing what they say is required.** Ask whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before your tenancy and whether you were told so. If not, ask them to show why professional cleaning is required to restore the pre-tenancy condition, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Gather evidence of the carpets' condition.** The condition report form recommends dated, labelled photos at the start and end of the tenancy, close-up and at a distance, identifying the room or location [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep your own photos, receipts for any cleaning products or equipment, and any notes on the carpets' state.
4. **Watch for bond claims.** Before a bond claim is made to the landlord, the landlord must give you "bond claim evidence" at least 3 days earlier, and it must not conflict with the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If a claim is made without your consent, you can notify the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 14 days that it is subject to a Tribunal application [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a professional receipt is required as evidence, or whether a self-clean can satisfy the term.
- Whether your 2024 lease form wording matches the current standard form.
- Whether your carpets were professionally cleaned before your tenancy began.

For a binding answer on the receipt, consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether an invoice sent after your full bond was returned is payable. They do show that cleaning costs are normally claimed from the bond, and that the landlord must follow a process to do so. Your verbal agreement to a bond deduction is not addressed in the retrieved material.

The current law is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Act version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), read with the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Renter's duty:** At the end of a tenancy, you must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **What a landlord can claim from the bond:** The landlord can claim the "reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Process for a bond claim:** At least 3 days before a claim for repayment to the landlord is made, the landlord must give the renter "bond claim evidence" that supports it. That evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A claim must be in a form approved by the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Signing a claim form:** A landlord must not request or obtain your signature on a claim form unless the form specifies the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Time limit for a Tribunal application:** A landlord's application to the Tribunal for a bond repayment order must be made within 14 days after the agreement terminates [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A claim made a month later may therefore be out of time for that route, though the documents don't say how this applies to a claim made directly to the Authority.
- **Further compensation:** A person who has already recovered compensation from a bond is not precluded from taking proceedings under Part 5 to recover an additional amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This suggests a landlord may still pursue extra cleaning costs through the Tribunal, but the documents don't say how a landlord would do so for a cleaning invoice.
- **Professional cleaning:** If the invoice is for professional cleaning, the landlord cannot require you to arrange it unless either professional cleaning was done before your tenancy started and you were told so, or it is needed to restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition, having regard to the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Your agreement and the invoice

The retrieved documents don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay an invoice, or whether a separate invoice is a debt you must pay. I can't answer that from these sources.

## What you can do

1. **Ask for the bond claim evidence and the condition report.** Check whether the cleaning charge is supported by the evidence and whether it conflicts with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for an itemised invoice and the cost basis.** The claim must be for a *reasonable* cost, so you can question the amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check whether a professional-cleaning requirement applied.** If the invoice is for professional cleaning, see the conditions in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Take legal advice or seek a Tribunal view** if the landlord pursues the invoice. The documents mention Tribunal applications but don't set out your deadlines to respond or dispute.

## Not covered by the documents

- Whether your verbal agreement to a bond deduction is binding.
- Whether an invoice issued after bond repayment is enforceable as a debt.
- How and when you must respond to an invoice or Tribunal claim.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't require you to wait indefinitely. The law lets you arrange urgent repairs yourself in some circumstances, but only if you meet specific conditions. Whether a broken tap counts as an urgent repair is not fully settled by the documents.

**Source:** The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **115** (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* are Authorised Version **009** (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Urgent repairs:** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and they are unable to get the provider or agent to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **What counts as urgent:** The definition includes a failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance provided for water, hot water, or cooking/heating by the residential rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It also lists a burst water service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether a single broken tap meets this definition is not addressed in the documents, so you would need to check that point.
- **Qualified tradespeople:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A "suitably qualified person" includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Written notice:** A renter must give written notice to the provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Reimbursement:** If you carry out the repairs, you must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to the prescribed amount, within 7 days after receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The prescribed amount is $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal:** You can apply to VCAT if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay the cost of urgent repairs you arranged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear that application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

1. **Put it in writing now.** Your two phone calls may not be enough. The law expects written notice, so email or write to the emergency contact and the provider, stating the fault and that you need it fixed immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Keep a record** of every call and message, including times, and the names of the people you spoke to. The documents do not define "reasonable steps," so this record is your evidence.
3. **Use a suitably qualified person** if you arrange the repair yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Keep the receipt and send the provider written notice** of the repair and its cost within 7 days of doing the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the provider refuses to pay,** you can apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether the owner can insist that only their own tradespeople carry out repairs. The documents do not address this.
- How long a renter must wait before the "unable to get the provider to repair" condition is met.
- Whether a single tap counts as an essential water service.

For guidance on urgent repairs, the Regulations point to consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the water is off to the whole house, consider contacting a licensed plumber now and documenting the cost and urgency.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, you can likely end the lease before moving in if the house is not in good repair or does not meet the rental minimum standards. The documents do not give you a right to a rent reduction for disrepair. They also do not say whether you can recover other costs, so get advice before relying on that.

Both documents are in force today (9 November 2026). The Act is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That copy does not carry an "Authorised Version" number, so I can only cite it as version 009.

## What the law says

- **Premises must be ready on move-in day.** The provider must ensure that on the agreed day the premises are vacant and reasonably clean. You are not required to move in if they are not, and you do not have to pay rent for the period between the agreed day and the day you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rental minimum standards.** The provider must ensure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under the regulations, the premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof," and "each room... must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber may bear on the structural soundness standard, but the documents do not say so expressly.
- **Good repair.** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit for occupation. This applies whether or not you knew of the disrepair before moving in, and despite the rent paid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** "Urgent repairs" include "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your options

**1. Cancel the lease**
- Because you have not entered possession, you may give notice of termination on the ground that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or do not meet the rental minimum standards. The agreement then terminates [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Alternatively, you may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation. The termination date "may be the date on which the notice is given or a later date" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The documents do not define "unfit for human habitation," so you should get the house professionally inspected and keep written evidence.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- Ask the provider for urgent repairs in writing. Section 65A(2) allows you to issue a request for urgent repairs if the premises do not comply with the standards on or immediately after the day you enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not clearly say whether this works before you move in, so take advice on timing.
- The regulations say that if you arrange urgent repairs yourself, you may be reimbursed "directly by the rental provider for the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500," and you may apply to VCAT if the cost is more than $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This wording is from the standard-form summary, and the documents do not confirm how it applies before move-in.
- For non-urgent repairs, you must notify the provider in writing. The provider must carry out the repairs in a reasonable time. You may apply to VCAT if they have not done so within 14 days of receiving notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Record the defects on the condition report. A condition report that is given to the provider is treated as notice of any defects or outstanding repairs it states [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate or incomplete condition report within 30 days after the agreement starts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
The documents do not contain a provision that lets you reduce rent because of disrepair. The only rent-related protection I found is that you do not have to pay rent for the period before you actually move in if the premises do not comply with the move-in requirements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The hardship provision for reducing a fixed term agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) requires an unforeseen change in your circumstances, so it does not appear to fit this situation. The documents do not cover whether you can negotiate or claim a rent reduction for the defects.

## Practical steps

- Put all complaints and any termination notice in writing and keep copies.
- Take dated photos of the damp, mould and timber damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Get a written report from a suitably qualified person, which may also help with any VCAT application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) or a community legal centre for advice before giving notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered by the documents:** whether you can recover costs such as removal or storage fees, the bond or rent you have already paid, or any compensation for the inconvenience. Please get advice on these.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Documents relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **No. 115** (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **No. 009** (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act is the primary source; the Regulations are a summary.

## What the law says

- **Urgent repairs** include a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must keep the premises in good repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The renter must give written notice of damage "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice now.** Tell the provider about the break-in damage to the plumbing and wiring as soon as practicable, in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Include the fact of the damage and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

2. **Arrange urgent repairs if the provider doesn't act.** You may do so only if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to repair immediately and they haven't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must then give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice, capped at the statutory amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary states that amount as up to $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

3. **Apply to VCAT.** You can apply for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot pay for them, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the provider doesn't reimburse you within 7 days of your written notice, you can seek a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

4. **End the lease early, if the damage is serious enough.** A renter may give notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe." The termination date may be the day of notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An ordinary notice cannot end a fixed term early [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether your damage meets this test is a factual question the documents don't resolve. You would need an assessment of the plumbing and wiring.

5. **Cleaning.** At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Professional cleaning can be required only to restore the condition from the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Burglary damage you can't clean may not fall under this, but the documents don't say so directly.

6. **Protect your bond and records.** The provider can claim bond for repair costs from renter-caused damage, and for cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep photos and written records. The provider must complete the condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends, and a condition report given to the provider counts as notice of defects [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

7. **Insurance.** A lease term cannot make you liable by default for the provider's insurance excess [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Who pays for damage caused by burglars.** The damage rules in the Act apply to the renter and visitors [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address third-party break-ins.
- **Police reports and insurance claims.** Not covered.
- **Lease-break fees for an early exit under this ground.** The documents address lease-break fees only in other circumstances [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Because the outcome depends on the extent of the damage, consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT promptly.

(2) Urgent repairs are defined to include a burst water service and a dangerous electrical fault, and the answer explains that the renter can arrange repairs and be reimbursed if the provider doesn't act. (3) The hardest point is covered by 'End the lease early, if the damage is serious enough. A renter may give notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation"... The termination date may be the day of notice or later.' The contrast with 'An ordinary notice cannot end a fixed term early' shows this ground works even during the fixed term.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never makes the renter liable for the burglary damage or binds them to stay, since it says 'The provider must keep the premises in good repair' and that 'A renter may give notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation"' even though 'An ordinary notice cannot end a fixed term early.'

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version No. 115' (link 97-109aa115), and it relies only on that version and on the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 'Authorised Version No. 009', which is the Regulations version in force, so no rule comes from an out-of-force version.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the retrieved law, a card surcharge is likely prohibited unless another Act permits it, and the documents do not say whether the payments company is an ADI. Who receives the fee does not change the analysis.

I applied the current version of the Act: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version (reprint) **No. 115**, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also relied on the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised version **No. 009**, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Fees for paying rent are prohibited.** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The prescribed matters include rent payment.** The regulations list "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter. This applies on and after 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **A fee-free method must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure that a rent payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost information must be given first.** The provider or agent must tell the renter about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, before the renter consents to a particular payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Centrepay and EFT must be allowed.** The provider must permit Centrepay, and electronic funds transfer is the prescribed payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

Not under these provisions. The fee prohibition applies to "a person" who demands or receives the fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The obligations to keep a free method available and to disclose costs apply to the provider or the provider's agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether a payments company acting for the agent is caught in the same way, so get that confirmed.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** whether the card fee is a payment surcharge permitted under another Act, and which Act. The documents do not identify any such Act.
2. **Ask whether the payments company is an ADI.** The exemption in section 51A only covers ADIs, and the documents don't say whether this company is one.
3. **Confirm the free bank transfer option.** Slower payment does not by itself breach the law, but the free method must be "reasonably available" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for the cost disclosure.** You are entitled to information about fees before you consent to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether the card fee is permitted under any other Act.
- Whether the payments company is an ADI.
- How to lodge a complaint or enforce these rules. The documents show penalties but not the complaint process.

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice.

must-mention.reason: Yes - all three points are covered: the free method must be 'reasonably available' (no extra costs apart from the renter's own bank fees); the answer says 'A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee' for rent payment, that rent payment is a prescribed matter 'other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act', and that 'Who receives the fee does not change the analysis' (the later suggestion to confirm whether the payments company is caught does not reverse that conclusion); and it gives next steps such as asking the agent in writing and confirming the free bank transfer option.

The answer never says the fee is allowed because a fee-free option exists, and never says the landlord or agent is exempt; instead it says 'A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent' and concludes 'Probably not.'

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version (reprint) No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026" and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "Authorised version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026" (links 97-109aa115 and 21-3sra009); both are the in-force versions, and no rule is drawn from any other version.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, you probably don't have to pay for a professional clean if your own cleaning restored the carpets to their move-in condition. The documents don't say whether an agent can insist on a professional receipt, so I can't confirm that point.

**Which law applies:** Today (9 November 2026), the relevant documents are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't include the version in force when your lease started in 2024, so I can't say whether your clause matches that version.

**What the law says**

- A standard-form lease can require professional cleaning or payment for it only if professional cleaning "becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed term says the renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises... having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless one of two conditions applies. One is that professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told so. The other is that professional cleaning is required to restore the premises, having regard to the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A term outside the standard form may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal can declare a term invalid or vary it if it is harsh or unconscionable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Ask the agent to show why professional cleaning is required.** The trigger is restoration to the move-in condition, not a receipt. Ask what specifically is not restored.
- **Check your condition report.** Within 10 days after the lease ends, the provider must complete the condition report with you present, or give you a reasonable chance to attend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A report signed by both of you is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition on the day stated [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the bond claim process.** The provider can claim the reasonable cost of cleaning only if the premises "were not left reasonably clean... having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Any bond claim evidence must be given to you at least 3 days before a claim is made, and it must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply to the Tribunal to challenge a term or dispute a claim [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Evidence that would help show the carpets' condition**

The documents specifically point to the condition report as the benchmark [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Beyond that, the documents don't list evidence types. These general suggestions are not from the documents:

- Your signed move-in condition report, and any notes you wrote on it.
- Dated photos or video of the carpets at move-out, taken before and after cleaning.
- Receipts for cleaning products or equipment you used.
- Any move-in cleaning records, if the agent gave you them.

**What the documents don't cover:** Whether a receipt from a professional is needed to prove compliance, what counts as "cleaning to a professional standard," and the wording of your 2024 lease. For a binding answer on your specific clause, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or seek legal advice.

(1) Reg 12: the provider 'must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning... unless' cleaning was done before the tenancy and the renter was told, or it is needed to restore the premises 'having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear'. (2) The s 63 duty is the hardest point because it appears only through the bond-claim provision, but the words 'were not left reasonably clean... having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement' still convey it. (3) The condition report is called 'the benchmark' and 'conclusive evidence of the premises' condition', and the answer also recommends the signed move-in condition report.

It says 'you probably don't have to pay for a professional clean if your own cleaning restored the carpets to their move-in condition' and that the trigger 'is restoration to the move-in condition, not a receipt.'

question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether an informal agreement to a cleaning deduction binds you to pay a later invoice. They do show that the agent's route to your bond runs through a formal claim, and that the agent can still seek extra compensation at the Tribunal after your bond is paid out. I can't confirm from these documents whether you must pay this invoice, so you should get tailored advice.

I checked the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both are current as of today.

### What the law says about cleaning and bonds

- **Cleaning is a valid bond claim in principle.** A provider may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Renters must leave premises reasonably clean.** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Formal claims need a form and evidence.** A claim for repayment to the provider must be made in an Authority-approved form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must give bond claim evidence (such as an invoice, receipt, quote, or photo) at least 3 days before the claim is made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A claim form must not be signed by renters unless it states the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter-signed claims are the mechanism for paying the provider.** A claim directing bond to the provider must be signed by the renters no earlier than 14 days before the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Does agreeing to a deduction mean agreeing to pay an invoice?

The documents don't answer this directly. The statutory process is built around a signed bond claim form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether a verbal or informal agreement creates a separate payment obligation is not covered in the documents I retrieved.

### The invoice after your bond was returned

- **The bond is generally no longer available.** Once the Authority has paid out a bond in good faith, "no further claim lies against the Authority" for that amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The agent can still seek compensation, but must go through the Tribunal.** A person who has recovered money from a bond "is not precluded from taking proceedings" under Part 5 to recover an additional amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A Tribunal may then order compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An invoice alone is not an order.
- **The Tribunal must consider money already taken from the bond.** It must consider "whether or not money has been paid to or recovered by the applicant by way of compensation, including money recovered or entitled to be recovered from the bond" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning has its own rules.** Under the Regulations, the provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either professional cleaning was done and you were told so before the tenancy started, or professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, taking into account the condition report and fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the invoice details and evidence.** Ask what was cleaned, why, and for the bond claim evidence (invoice, receipt, quote, or photos).
2. **Check the condition report.** Bond claim evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check whether the premises were reasonably clean.** Compare the condition at your move-out with the condition report at the start [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check whether any professional cleaning was required.** Look at whether the Regulations' conditions were met [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the agent applies to the Tribunal,** you can respond there, and the Tribunal will weigh the matters in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), including the amount already recovered from your bond.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents suggest you don't have to wait indefinitely. If the problem is an urgent repair, you may be able to arrange a suitably qualified tradesperson yourself and seek reimbursement, but only after taking specific steps. The documents don't set a fixed waiting period.

It also includes "a failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A suitably qualified person includes a registered or licensed tradesperson for the relevant work [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Renter's right to arrange repairs:** A renter "may arrange for urgent repairs to be done if the renter has taken reasonable steps to arrange for the rental provider to immediately do the repairs and the rental provider has not carried out the repairs" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Victorian law requires the landlord to deliver the home in a condition that meets the rental minimum standards, including free of mould and damp. You can ask for urgent repairs and can refuse to move in until the home is fixed. The documents I found do not clearly confirm that you can cancel the lease or reduce your rent for these defects, so those points need further advice.

## What the law says

- **Landlord's duty before you move in:** The provider must ensure the rented premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation [2, s 65A(1)]. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person [2, s 65A(1)].
- **Standards that apply to your situation:** The premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof," and "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [1, Sch 4, cls 7–8].
- **Rotting timber:** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes a fault or damage that makes premises "unsafe or insecure," including "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure," and "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [2, s 3(1)].
- **You don't have to move in:** The premises must be vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed day. If they are not, you are "not required to enter into occupation" [2, s 65(1)–(2)]. You also don't have to pay rent for the period between the agreed day and when you actually move in [2, s 65(3)].
- **Repairs duty applies regardless of what you knew:** The provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," whether or not you were aware of the disrepair before entering, and despite the rent or the age of the building [2, s 68(1), (1A)].

## What you can do

**1. Ask for repairs (in writing)**
- Give written notice of the damage as soon as practicable [2, s 72AA].
- If the home doesn't meet the standards, you may issue a request for urgent repairs [2, s 65A(2)]. Note that this request right is tied to the point you enter occupation, so raise it in writing now and keep records.
- If the provider can't be reached to fix urgent repairs, you may arrange them yourself after taking reasonable steps to get the provider to act immediately. You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to the prescribed amount [2, s 72(1)–(2)]. The regulations' summary says this is "up to $2500" [1, Sch 1, Form 2 Part D, item 30].
- You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay [2, s 73(1)]. VCAT must hear this within 2 business days [2, s 73(2)].
- For non-urgent repairs, you must give written notice. If repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can apply to the Director or VCAT [2, ss 74–75].

**2. Record the condition**
- Under the condition report rules, you should note anything unsafe or needing repair, and take dated photos [1, Sch 1, Form 4, paras 4, 1]. You have 5 business days after moving in to complete and sign the report [1, Sch 1, Form 4, para 3]. If you later find problems, you can apply to VCAT to correct the report within 30 days after the agreement's start date [1, Sch 1, Form 4, para 5].

**3. Cancel the lease: not confirmed**
- The Regulations' form notes a notice of intention to vacate on the basis that premises are "destroyed or unfit for habitation" under s 91ZD of the Act [1, Sch 1, Form 2, cl 16.3(a)]. However, the text of s 91ZD itself is not in the documents I retrieved, so I can't confirm when you qualify or how to give that notice. Get advice before relying on this.

**4. Reduce rent: only partly answered**
- The clearest rent point is that you don't pay rent for the period before you actually move in, as noted above [2, s 65(3)].
- For ongoing defects, the documents mention paying rent into the Rent Special Account if the provider fails to carry out repairs, and the Tribunal can order payment of rent into that account [2, s 77(1)–(2)]. This holds rent rather than reducing it, and the documents don't show a general rent-reduction right. The Tribunal's power to order a rent refund (s 48) is listed but its text isn't in the excerpts I retrieved.

## Version of the law

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997:** Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [2, cover page].
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021:** S.R. No. 3/2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't state an "Authorised Version No." for the Regulations, so I can't give that number.

These are the latest versions in the documents as at today, 9 November 2026.

---

**Next steps:** Notify the landlord or agent in writing today, listing each defect and attaching photos. Keep copies. Then contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181, consumer.vic.gov.au/renting) [1, Sch 1, Form 1, Part D] or a tenants' legal service before deciding whether to cancel or claim rent back. This is general information, not legal advice.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** Tell your landlord in writing now, and ask for urgent repairs, because a burst water service or dangerous electrical fault is an urgent repair under the Act. If they don't act, you may be able to arrange the repairs yourself and seek reimbursement. Ending the lease early is only realistic if the premises are unfit or unsafe. The documents don't say whether the landlord must pay for damage caused by burglars.

**Sources:** This answer uses the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both are the current versions as of today.

---

## What the law says

- **Written notice:** You must give written notice to the landlord "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** Urgent repairs include work to repair "a burst water service" or "a dangerous electrical fault", and "serious storm or fire damage" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your damage duty:** The rule against damage applies to "a renter and any visitor", and fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglars are not obviously "visitors" (a visitor is someone on the premises "with the permission of the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)), but the documents don't address third-party damage directly.
- **Cleaning:** At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Professional cleaning can only be required if needed to restore the premises to their starting condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs by a qualified person:** "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do before the lease ends

1. **Notify in writing today.** Describe the damage (plumbing, wiring, break-ins) and ask for urgent repairs. Keep a copy.
2. **Use the urgent repairs process.** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have "taken reasonable steps to arrange for" the landlord to repair immediately and you cannot get them done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must then give the landlord "7 days written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice, and the amount is capped at the lesser of the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The prescribed amount is "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply for an urgent repairs order if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application "within 2 business days" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** If some items are not urgent, give written notice. If the landlord hasn't acted within 14 days, you can apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** After giving a repair notice, you may apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord fails to carry out repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Ending the lease early.** You may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe". The termination date can be the date of the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Otherwise, a notice must give at least 28 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and a notice specifying an end date earlier than the end of a fixed term is of no effect in the general case [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). With about three weeks left, the general route would not end the lease sooner.
7. **Protect your bond and evidence.** Complete the condition report, take dated photos, and note the damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The landlord must complete the end-of-tenancy inspection and condition report within 10 days after the lease ends, and give you a chance to attend [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Any bond claim for cleaning or repairs must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether the landlord must pay for damage caused by burglars.
- Police reports or insurance claims.
- Whether the damage makes the premises "unsafe" enough to support a notice under the destroyed/unsafe ground.
- Whether a lease break fee applies in that case.

For advice, the Regulations list Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the app probably cannot charge you a card fee for rent, unless the fee is a "payment surcharge" permitted under another Act, which the documents don't identify. Whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent doesn't change the basic rule.

**Documents relied on:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* ("the Act"), title "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026, Authorised Version 115 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* ("the Regulations"), title "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", in force from 30 June 2026, Authorised Version 009 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both are the latest versions retrieved, so they are the versions in force today, 9 November 2026.

### What the law says

- **Fees for paying rent are prohibited.** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations list "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 penalty units for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The exception is unclear.** The "payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act" exception depends on another Act, and the documents don't say whether any such Act covers card fees. I can't confirm that your card fee falls within it.
- **The provider or agent must offer a no-extra-cost method.** The provider or agent must ensure that a rent payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed.** Before the renter consents to a payment method, the provider or agent must give information about any costs the renter may incur, including third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Electronic funds transfer is the prescribed method.** For the purposes of the Act, the prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether your manual bank transfer counts as this, though it may.

### Does it matter who gets the fee?

For the fee prohibition, the documents don't limit it to the landlord or agent. Section 51A applies to "a person" other than an ADI [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so the payments company may also be caught. For the no-extra-cost obligation and the disclosure duty, the obligation is on the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because your agent uses the payments company, the agent is still responsible for making a free method reasonably available, even if the fee is charged by a third party.

### What you can do or ask

- Ask your agent in writing whether the card fee is a "payment surcharge fee permitted under any other Act," and which Act they rely on.
- Ask for the cost information the agent must give you before you consent to the card option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Confirm that the free bank transfer option is available and, if the agent says it isn't, ask why.

**Not covered:** The documents don't set out how to enforce this rule, who to complain to, or whether the bank transfer's slower speed affects the agent's obligations. They also don't say whether the app's terms or the payments company's fees are lawful beyond what is quoted above. For enforcement steps, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT), but those sources are not in the retrieved documents.

question: My lease is on the standard form and started in 2024. It has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Not automatically. Under the current law, you must pay for professional cleaning only if it is actually needed to restore the carpets to their condition at the start of the tenancy, taking fair wear and tear into account. The documents I found do not say who decides that, or what proof an agent must accept.

I answered from the versions in force today: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (in force 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (in force 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The file metadata gives these version numbers. The documents do not show the wording that applied when your lease began in 2024.

---

### What the law says

- A standard-form lease may include a term requiring professional cleaning, but only if professional cleaning "becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord must not require professional cleaning at the end unless either the premises were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told so, or professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their starting condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, fair wear and tear excepted [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A landlord can claim from the bond the reasonable cost of cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, "having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" of the agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Applying this to you

- If your carpets are back to their starting condition, the test for requiring professional cleaning may not be met. The documents do not say whether a self-clean can satisfy the clause, so the question is factual.
- Check whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in and whether you were told. If they were not, and you were not told, the landlord cannot require professional cleaning at all [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What would help show the carpets' condition

- **Your start-of-tenancy condition report.** It should list floor coverings [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Form 4 says the report "will help to resolve disputes over cleaning, damage, safety or missing items" and that you should comment on anything you disagree with [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Photos at the start and end of the tenancy.** The form advises dated, labelled, close-up and distance photos, identified by room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The end-of-tenancy inspection.** The landlord must complete the final condition report within 10 days after the end date, give you a chance to attend if possible, and allow for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A signed condition report is conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition on the day specified in it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your own records of the clean,** such as receipts, products used, and dated photos. The documents do not say what evidence an agent must accept.

### What you can ask or do

1. **Ask the agent in writing** which carpet areas they say are not restored, and why professional cleaning is "required" to restore them under the condition report.
2. **Ask to attend the final inspection** and record any disagreement on the report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **If the landlord claims your bond,** they must give you bond claim evidence at least 3 days before the claim, and that evidence must not conflict with a statement in the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **If you dispute a bond claim,** you can notify the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority in writing within 14 days that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application, which stops automatic payment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered by the documents:** whether an agent can insist on a receipt from a professional cleaner, what proof is sufficient, and how the law read in 2024. For a dispute, consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.
