question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond, but I never signed a bond claim form for it. Then my full bond came back to me, and a month later the agent sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether you must pay a separate invoice sent after your full bond was refunded, and they don't say whether agreeing verbally to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay an invoice. They do set out what a landlord or agent may claim for cleaning and how bond claims are made.

## What the law says

- **Cleaning is a permitted bond claim.** The landlord may claim for "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [1, s 411AB(1)(c)].
- **Renters must leave the premises reasonably clean.** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as at move-in, allowing for fair wear and tear [1, s 63(2)].
- **Bond claims follow a formal process.** A claim must be in a form approved by the Authority [1, s 411(2)(a)]. At least 3 days before a claim is made to the landlord, the landlord or agent must give the renter bond claim evidence supporting it [1, s 411(1A)]. The landlord must not request or obtain a renter's signature on a claim form unless the form states the amount to be refunded and any apportionment [1, s 411(5)].
- **Agents are covered.** The definition of "residential rental provider" includes "an agent of a residential rental provider" [1, s 404].
- **Professional cleaning has limits.** The landlord must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless the conditions in the regulations are met [2, reg 12(1)]. A term requiring the renter to pay for professional cleaning is a prohibited term unless it is in the standard form [1, s 27B(1)(d)–(e)].
- **Inspection duties apply.** The landlord or agent must complete the final inspection and condition report "within 10 days after the end date of the agreement" and give the renter "an opportunity to attend the inspection if possible" [2, Form 4, item 6].

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the evidence.** Request the invoice, the work done, and any photos or bond claim evidence. Ask whether a bond claim form was ever submitted to the Authority, and whether bond claim evidence was given to you at least 3 days beforehand [1, s 411(1A)].
2. **Check the condition report.** Compare the end-of-tenancy report with the start-of-tenancy report. A signed condition report is conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition on the day specified in it [1, s 36(1)]. Also check whether you were given the chance to attend the final inspection [2, Form 4].
3. **Check whether the cleaning was professional.** If the invoice is for professional cleaning, check whether reg 12 was met [2, reg 12].
4. **Keep records.** Your agreement to the deduction may matter, but the documents don't say whether an informal or verbal agreement creates a binding obligation to pay an invoice.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether you must pay a separate invoice issued after your bond was fully refunded.
- Whether your verbal agreement to a bond deduction binds you to pay a separate invoice.
- How a landlord recovers cleaning costs outside the bond process. The table of contents lists related provisions (for example, s 209 on compensation for breach of duty and s 213B on applications for loss or damage), but their text is not in the retrieved material, so I can't explain them.

For advice on your specific situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf), S.R. No. 3/2021, Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. I've called them twice today. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't necessarily have to wait. Under the law, you may be able to arrange the urgent repair yourself and seek reimbursement, but only if certain conditions are met. The documents don't confirm whether a burst pipe that cuts off water to the whole house counts as an urgent repair. I've relied on the current versions: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Urgent repairs:** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider or agent to do them immediately, and they cannot get the provider or agent to carry out the repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations give the example of "a burst water service" as an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). However, the documents I retrieved don't contain the full statutory definition of "urgent repairs," so check consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do the work:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The provider must also ensure anyone doing repair work is suitably qualified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So if you arrange the repair, it should be done by a qualified tradesperson, not by you personally.
- **Reimbursement:** The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost of the repairs, or the prescribed amount if lower [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations set the limit at $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The provider must reimburse within 7 days of receiving your written notice of the repairs and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do now

1. **Give written notice now.** You must notify the provider in writing as soon as practicable after becoming aware of a breakdown [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your two phone calls are useful, but put the report in writing too, and keep a copy.
2. **Keep a record of your attempts.** The "reasonable steps" test requires you to show you tried to get the provider or agent to act immediately [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how many attempts count, so keep notes of times, names, and responses.
3. **If the repair is urgent and no one comes, arrange a suitably qualified person.** Get a quote and the invoice.
4. **Notify the provider in writing within 7 days of the repair** of the repairs carried out and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Claim reimbursement.** The provider must pay within 7 days of your written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The reimbursement is capped at $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **If the provider refuses to pay, or you can't afford the cost, apply to VCAT.** You can apply if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **How long the provider has to attend.** The documents don't say how soon "immediately" means, or how many attempts are "reasonable."
- **Whether an owner's refusal to use any other tradesperson changes the position.** The documents don't address this directly.
- **Whether a whole-house water shut-off is an urgent repair** under the statutory definition.

This is general information, not legal advice. If the provider disputes your claim, consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** You may be able to end the agreement before moving in, and you can require repairs. The documents I found do not give you a right to a rent reduction for these defects.

I've checked both instruments in force today (9 November 2026): the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), in the version dated 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Regulations excerpt does not state an Authorised Version number.

## What the law says about your situation

- **Mould and damp:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The premises must also be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Rotting timber:** This likely falls under the structural soundness standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say expressly whether rot counts as a "structural" defect, so that point is an inference.
- **Urgent repairs:** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" and "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty to report:** You must give written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your move-in terms:** The lease form says the start date "is the date the agreement starts and you may move in" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are "vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Your options

**1. Cancel (end the agreement before moving in)**
- Under s 91L, an agreement terminates if you have not entered into possession and you give a notice of termination on the ground that the premises "are not in good repair," "are unfit for human habitation," or "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The documents do not define "entered into possession." Having picked up the keys without moving in or staying may or may not count, so this is a key point to check.
- The documents don't say how much notice is required under s 91L or what form the notice must take.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Written notice first:** Notify the provider in writing, as soon as practicable, of the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken "reasonable steps" to get the provider to do them immediately and the provider is unable or unwilling to do so [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must then reimburse "the reasonable cost of the repairs," within 7 days of written notice of the repairs and cost, capped at the amount in the Act, which is less than or equal to the prescribed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations prescribe reimbursement "up to $2500" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** If the provider doesn't act within 14 days of your written notice, you can apply to the Director to investigate under s 74 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) or to VCAT under s 75 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear a s 75 application within 7 days of it being made [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **VCAT orders:** VCAT can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 76(1)).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents do not provide a direct rent reduction for defects. I did not find a provision allowing you to reduce the rent for these conditions.
- The closest provision is s 77: you can apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if you have given notice requiring repairs and the provider has failed to carry out the duty to repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That holds rent, but it does not reduce it.
- VCAT's power to order compensation under s 76 may be a related route [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but the documents don't say how compensation is calculated for rent.

## What I couldn't find

- The text of s 65A (occupation of premises that do not comply with the rental minimum standards) and s 65 (provider's duty) was not in the results I retrieved. Those provisions may be relevant.
- Whether "unfit for human habitation" applies to your conditions is not defined in the excerpts I retrieved.
- Notice periods and forms for a s 91L termination are not in the excerpts.

## Suggested next steps

1. Put your complaint in writing now, listing the mould, damp and rotting timber, and attach photos. Note that the condition report is important: you can ask VCAT to amend an inaccurate or incomplete condition report within 30 days after the agreement starts [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 35A).
2. Decide whether you want to end the lease (s 91L) or stay and require repairs.
3. Get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service before serving a termination notice, given the open question about "possession."

The answer also explains s 91L termination before possession on minimum-standards, good-repair or habitability grounds, and the urgent-repair route (which includes minimum-standard failures) alongside non-urgent repairs.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and there are about three weeks left on our fixed-term lease. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, you should first report the damage to your landlord in writing. If the damage is an urgent repair, you may be able to arrange repairs and claim the cost back. You may also be able to give notice to leave early if the premises are unsafe. The documents I found don't cover every part of your situation, which I note below.

**Governing version:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* is in Authorised Version **No. 115**, in force from **13 October 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is the version in force today (9 November 2026). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 009, dated 30 June 2026) also apply [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Damage must be reported.** A renter must give written notice to the landlord "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs are defined.** These include "a burst water service," "a dangerous electrical fault," and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Break-in damage to plumbing and wiring may fall within these categories, but that depends on the facts.
- **Your right to arrange repairs.** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and you cannot get them done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to the prescribed amount, within 7 days after receiving written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations state the reimbursement cap is **$2,500** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Leaving early because of unsafe premises.** A renter may give notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or have been "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe." The termination date may be the day the notice is given or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Standard early exit.** A general notice of intention to vacate must give at least 28 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For a fixed-term agreement, a notice that ends the lease before the end of the term is of no effect in most cases [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). With about three weeks left, this route is unlikely to work.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Report in writing now.** Send the landlord or agent a written notice describing the break-in damage to the plumbing and wiring. Keep a copy and any proof of delivery [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** Request that the plumbing and electrical faults be repaired immediately. If the landlord does not act, you may arrange the repairs yourself, give 7 days' written notice of the cost, and seek reimbursement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Escalate if needed.** If the landlord refuses to pay, or you cannot meet the cost, you can apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the cost is above $2,500 or the landlord refuses to pay, the Regulations also allow a VCAT application [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Consider leaving early.** If the premises are unfit for habitation or unsafe, you may give a notice of intention to vacate under the destroyed-or-unsafe provision described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Get written evidence of the unsafe condition, such as a licensed tradesperson's report, before you rely on it.
5. **Cleaning.** You cannot be required to do professional cleaning unless the premises need it to be restored to their condition at the start of the tenancy, with fair wear and tear taken into account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the damage stops you from cleaning, say so in writing. The documents do not say how this applies where a third party caused the damage.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether a police report or an insurance claim is needed, or how it affects your position.
- Whether the three weeks left on your fixed term change the outcome of a s 91ZD notice.
- Security measures after the break-ins, beyond the general rules on locks and the Tribunal process for changing them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Whether a landlord may claim the cost of burglary damage from your bond. The bond provisions cover damage caused by the renter or a visitor [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and burglars are not visitors in the ordinary sense.

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For your specific situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.
